the incidence of an STI was 1.8 per 100 person‐years, and that the factors associated with an STI were being male, having a lower CD4 count, and having a higher viral load.
we found a higher risk of STIs in younger individuals and those of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander descent, those with a history of STIs and those who reported having sex with men and women.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the risk factors for incident STIs are age, male gender, being Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander, having sex with men (MSM), having a history of injecting drug use, having a history of STI, having a history HIV‐positive partner, and having a history of HIV‐positive partner with an STI.

the risk factors associated with an incident STI in HIV-positive patients in the Australian database were as follows: being male, having a CD4 cell count of 200–350 cells/µl, having an HIV RNA level of 100,000–500,000 copies/ml, being on antiretroviral therapy, and being on a protease inhibitor.
the study did not find any association between incident STIs and any of the factors assessed.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there is an urgent need to develop and evaluate effective interventions to reduce sexual risk behavior in HIV‐positive people.
the incidence of STIs is high among HIV‐positive patients.
the incidence of STIs in the HIV-positive population is higher than the general population, and the incidence is increasing.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there are a range of factors that are associated with an incident STI in HIV-positive individuals.
the majority of STIs in HIV‐positive men who have sex with men can be prevented through consistent condom use.
there is a lot of variation in the risk of acquiring an STI, even within this cohort of HIV‐positive people who are at high risk.
